Let $(\Omega,\mathfrak F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space
([[def-probability-measure]]), let $m\ge1$, and let
$X:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be a random element with target
$(\mathbb R^m,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m))$ ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]).
Use the statistical one-based coordinate labels: for every $v\in\mathbb R^m$
write $v_i:=v(i-1)$ for $1\le i\le m$, so
$X_i(\omega)=X(\omega)(i-1)$. Each $X_i$ is a real random variable because
the coordinate projection $x\mapsto x(i-1)$ is continuous and therefore has
Borel preimages of Borel sets
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]).
For every integer $r\ge1$ and matrix
$A\in M_{r\times m}(\mathbb R)$, the notation $A_{ij}$ below means its
zero-based matrix entry
$A(i-1,j-1)$ for $1\le i\le r$ and
$1\le j\le m$; likewise $\Sigma_{ij}$ means the entry at $(i-1,j-1)$ in
the covariance matrix below in the matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]]. These
are labels for the root library's zero-based function entries, not a different
matrix convention. If $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is open, $h:U\to\mathbb R^r$
has all first partials at $a\in U$, and $A=Jh(a)$, then $A_{ij}$ in this
notation is $\partial_{j-1}h_{i-1}(a)$, with the zero-based Jacobian
convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].
Assume $X$ is **square-integrable**:
$$E\bigl[|X|^2\bigr]=\sum_{i=1}^{m}E\bigl[X_i^2\bigr]<+\infty ,$$
where $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
Its **mean vector** is
$$\mu=E[X]:=\bigl(E[X_1],\dots,E[X_m]\bigr)\in\mathbb R^m ,$$
the coordinates being the expectations of
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. Its **covariance matrix** is the
$m\times m$ real matrix of [[def-matrix-space]]
$$\Sigma=\operatorname{Cov}(X):=\bigl(\Sigma_{ij}\bigr)_{i,j=1}^{m},\qquad \Sigma_{ij}:=E\bigl[(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)\bigr]\in\mathbb R .$$
For the random vector $X$ the entries $\Sigma_{ij}$ are also written
$\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)$, and $\Sigma_{ii}=\operatorname{Var}(X_i)$.

### Well-definedness and elementary properties

**Integrability of the entries.** Square-integrability gives
$E[X_i^2]<+\infty$ for each $i$. Since the underlying measure is a
probability measure, the elementary inequality
$$|X_i|\le \tfrac12\bigl(1+X_i^2\bigr)$$
gives $E|X_i|\le\tfrac12(1+E[X_i^2])<+\infty$ by monotonicity and
homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]); hence $X_i$
is integrable and $\mu_i=E[X_i]$ is finite
([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]). Also
$$(X_i-\mu_i)^2\le2X_i^2+2\mu_i^2,$$
so $X_i-\mu_i$ is square-integrable; the probability-space inequality
$$|X_i-\mu_i|\le\tfrac12\bigl(1+(X_i-\mu_i)^2\bigr)$$
then makes it integrable as well. Finally
$$|(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)|\le \tfrac12\bigl((X_i-\mu_i)^2+(X_j-\mu_j)^2\bigr),$$
and the right-hand side is integrable by additivity, monotonicity and
homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]],
[[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]); hence every
$\Sigma_{ij}$ is a finite real number.

**Symmetry.** For all $i,j$ the real numbers $(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)$ and
$(X_j-\mu_j)(X_i-\mu_i)$ are equal pointwise, so $\Sigma_{ij}=\Sigma_{ji}$;
thus $\Sigma^{\mathsf T}=\Sigma$.

For $M\in M_{m\times m}(\mathbb R)$ and $z\in\mathbb R^m$, write
$$z^{\mathsf T}Mz:=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}z_iM_{ij}z_j.$$
For a real symmetric $m\times m$ matrix $M$, **positive semidefinite** means
$z^{\mathsf T}Mz\ge0$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^m$, and **positive definite**
means $z^{\mathsf T}Mz>0$ for every nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^m$. For a real
random variable $Z$, **almost surely constant** means that $Z=c$ outside a
measurable $\mathbb P$-null set for some $c\in\mathbb R$
([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).

**Positive semidefiniteness.** Let $z=(z_1,\dots,z_m)\in\mathbb R^m$. The
random variable $W:=\sum_{i=1}^{m}z_iX_i$ is a finite linear combination of
square-integrable random variables, hence square-integrable, and bilinearity
of covariance ([[lem-variance-and-covariance-identities-for-random-variables]])
gives
$$z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z=\sum_{i,j=1}^{m}z_iz_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j) =\operatorname{Cov}(W,W)=\operatorname{Var}(W) =E\bigl[(W-E[W])^2\bigr]\ge0 ,$$
the inequality holding because $(W-E[W])^2\ge0$ pointwise and expectation is
monotone ([[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]]). If
$z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z=\operatorname{Var}(W)=0$, Chebyshev's inequality gives
$\mathbb P(|W-E[W]|\ge1/r)=0$ for every integer $r\ge1$; the union of these
events is $\{W\ne E[W]\}$, so $W=E[W]$ almost surely
([[cor-chebyshev-inequality-for-random-variables]]). Conversely, if $W=c$
almost surely, invariance of the integral under almost-everywhere equality
gives $E[W]=c$ and $E[(W-E[W])^2]=0$
([[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]). Hence
$z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z=0$ exactly when $W$ is almost surely constant, and
$\Sigma$ is positive definite exactly when for every $z\ne0$ the random
variable $\sum_{i=1}^{m}z_iX_i$ fails to be almost surely constant.

No independence hypothesis is used anywhere in this definition; $\Sigma$
records the pairwise covariances of the coordinates.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

For a fixed $\rho$, write $Z_1=Z_x(\rho)$ and $Z_2=Z_y(\rho)$. The
diagonal products $|Z_j|^2$ are integrable by the given finite second moment,
and
$|Z_1\overline{Z_2}|=|Z_1||Z_2|\le(|Z_1|^2+|Z_2|^2)/2$
pointwise. Hence each entry $\mathbb E[Z_i\overline{Z_j}]$ is a finite complex
expectation under [F1]–[F2], so $\Gamma(\rho)$ is well-defined.

Componentwise conjugation and linearity of the real integrals give
$\Gamma_{ji}=\mathbb E[Z_j\overline{Z_i}]
=\mathbb E[\overline{Z_i\overline{Z_j}}]
=\overline{\mathbb E[Z_i\overline{Z_j}]}=\overline{\Gamma_{ij}}$;
the diagonal entries are real and nonnegative. Therefore
$\Gamma^\dagger=\Gamma$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and $\omega>0$, let $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$,
and let $(E,B)$ be the plane-wave pair of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] on
the whole-space region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$, with phase
$\theta(x,t)=k\cdot x-\omega t$. Suppose the amplitude conditions of
[[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] hold, so that $k\cdot e=0$ and
$b=k\times e/\omega$. By that theorem, if the pair is nonzero then it also
satisfies the dispersion relation $|k|=\omega/c$, while the zero pair is
permitted for every $k\ne0$ and $\omega>0$, both on and off this dispersion
relation. This item classifies the polarization of that class of transverse
plane waves; it adds no field-theoretic content.

Write $e=a+id$ with the real vectors $a=\operatorname{Re}e$ and
$d=\operatorname{Im}e$ of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]],
applied componentwise in $\mathbb C^3$; since $k$ is real and $k\cdot e=0$, the
real and imaginary parts of this complex equation give
$\langle k,a\rangle=\langle k,d\rangle=0$. Put $\hat k=k/|k|$, and let
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$, $|\cdot|$ and $\times$ be the inner product, norm
and cross product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and
[[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. Then:

(a) [Trace] At every fixed $x$ one has
$E(x,t)=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$ with $\theta=\theta(x,t)$. The curve
$\gamma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$, $\gamma(\theta):=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$,
lies in the transverse plane
$k^\perp=\{v\in\mathbb R^3:\langle k,v\rangle=0\}$; it is the image of the unit
circle $S^1=\{(u_1,u_2)\in\mathbb R^2:u_1^2+u_2^2=1\}$ under the $\mathbb R$-linear
map $(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$; it is $2\pi$-periodic in the phase parameter
$\theta$ and satisfies $\gamma(\theta+\pi)=-\gamma(\theta)$, while the map
$t\mapsto E(x,t)$ has time period $T=2\pi/\omega$. The curve $\gamma$ is
called the **polarization trace** at $x$; it does not depend on $x$, so the
classification below is the same at every point.

(b) [Classification] Exactly one of the following three cases holds.

(i) **Linear polarization**: $\dim_{\mathbb R}\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}\le1$.
When $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=1$, the trace is a nontrivial closed
segment in that span, traversed twice per period; when $a=d=0$, the trace is
the single point $\{0\}$ and $(E,B)$ is the zero wave.

(ii) **Circular polarization**: $|a|=|d|>0$ and $\langle a,d\rangle=0$. The
trace is the circle of radius $|a|$ in $k^\perp$, and $|E(x,t)|=|a|$ for all
$(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$.

(iii) **Elliptical (nondegenerate, noncircular) polarization**:
$\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=2$ and not (ii). Here a **nondegenerate ellipse centred at $0$** in a real plane $P$ means
the set $L(S^1)$ for a real-linear isomorphism $L:\mathbb R^2\to P$.
The trace is such an ellipse in $\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}$, and the
origin lies in the relative interior of the enclosed region
$L(\{u\in\mathbb R^2:|u|\le1\})$ in that plane. If in addition $\langle a,d\rangle=0$, the
parametrization is along principal axes and the semiaxis lengths are $|a|$ and
$|d|$; the general principal-axis computation is not asserted by this item.

(c) [Handedness] For $a,d\in k^\perp$, the cross product $a\times d$ is
orthogonal to $a$ and to $d$
([[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]), hence parallel
to $k$; define the **helicity sign**
$H:=\langle a\times d,\hat k\rangle\in\mathbb R$, whose sign is taken in the
order of [[def-real-order]]. One has $H=0$ exactly in the linear case (i), and
$H\ne0$ otherwise. This library calls the polarization **right-handed** when
$H<0$ and **left-handed** when $H>0$. Geometrically, $H<0$ means that at fixed
$x$ the electric vector rotates clockwise as seen by an observer facing the
incoming wave (looking along $-\hat k$), and $H>0$ means counterclockwise;
here the screen orientation is fixed by any positive orthonormal triad
$(u,v,\hat k)$, with $u$ to the right and $v$ up for that observer.
Equivalently, $\langle E(x,t)\times\partial_tE(x,t),\hat k\rangle=\omega H$ for
every $(x,t)$. The names "right" and "left" handedness are conventional and
both conventions occur in the literature, so later statements in this library
use only the sign of $H$.

(d) [Status] This is a classification definition. It introduces the trace,
the three cases and the sign $H$, and asserts no field equation, no
propagation, energy or empirical content. The magnetic amplitude enters only
through the two amplitude conditions $k\cdot e=0$ and $b=k\times e/\omega$
recalled above; the definition covers the zero wave, both on and off the
dispersion relation, and no non-plane or non-transverse field is classified.

### Well-definedness and conventions

The real vectors $a,d$ are well defined by the componentwise real and
imaginary parts of $e$; because $k$ is real, taking real and imaginary parts of
$k\cdot e=\sum_jk_j(a_j+id_j)$ gives $\langle k,a\rangle=0$ and
$\langle k,d\rangle=0$, so $a,d\in k^\perp$ and $\gamma$ takes values in
$k^\perp$. The trace formula in (a) is Euler's formula
$\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ of [[thm-eulers-formula]] together with
the field arithmetic on the right-hand side of
$E=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((a+id)(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\bigr)
=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta)+i(a\sin\theta+d\cos\theta)\bigr)$
and the real-linearity of $\operatorname{Re}$: the real part is
$a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$, while the imaginary part is not a field. Since
$\theta(x,t)=k\cdot x-\omega t$ and $\omega>0$, at fixed $x$ the map
$t\mapsto\theta$ is a bijection onto $\mathbb R$; hence the set traced by
$E(x,t)$ as $t$ varies is the full image $\gamma(\mathbb R)$, independently of
$x$, and $\gamma$ is $2\pi$-periodic with $\gamma(\theta+\pi)=-\gamma(\theta)$
because $\cos$ and $\sin$ shift by a sign under $\theta\mapsto\theta+\pi$. The
time period is $T=2\pi/\omega$, the least positive $s$ with
$\theta(x,t+s)=\theta(x,t)-2\pi$ for all $(x,t)$; it is distinct from the
phase-parameter period $2\pi$ of $\gamma$.

For the classification, "exactly one of the three cases holds" is checked
case by case: if $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}\le1$ then (i); otherwise
$\dim=2$, and either $|a|=|d|>0$ with $\langle a,d\rangle=0$, which is (ii),
or not, which is (iii). In case (i) with $\dim=1$, write $d=\lambda a$ with
$a\ne0$ (or symmetrically $a=\mu d$); then
$\gamma(\theta)=(\cos\theta-\lambda\sin\theta)a$, whose image is the segment
$\{sa:|s|\le\sqrt{1+\lambda^2}\}$ in $\mathbb R a$, traversed once in each direction between successive extrema of the scalar
factor (each such phase interval has length $\pi$). In case (ii),
expanding with the bilinearity of the inner product
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) gives
$|u_1a-u_2d|^2=u_1^2|a|^2+u_2^2|d|^2-2u_1u_2\langle a,d\rangle=|a|^2$
whenever $|a|=|d|$, $\langle a,d\rangle=0$ and $u_1^2+u_2^2=1$, so the image
of the unit circle under $(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$ is contained in the
circle of radius $|a|$ in the plane $\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}$; conversely,
for every $v$ in that plane with $|v|=|a|$ the coordinates
$u_1=\langle v,a\rangle/|a|^2$ and $u_2=-\langle v,d\rangle/|d|^2$ satisfy
$u_1^2+u_2^2=1$ and $u_1a-u_2d=v$, because $a/|a|$ and $d/|d|$ are orthonormal
and $v=\langle v,a/|a|\rangle(a/|a|)+\langle v,d/|d|\rangle(d/|d|)$; hence the
trace is exactly that circle. In case (iii) the vectors $a,d$
are linearly independent, so $T:(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$ is a linear
isomorphism of $\mathbb R^2$ onto the two-dimensional plane
$\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}$; the image of the closed unit disk under $T$ is a
compact convex subset with nonempty interior in that plane, the image of the
open disk is its nonempty interior, and the image of the unit circle is its
boundary, so the trace is a nondegenerate ellipse centred at
$0=T(0)$ with the origin in the relative interior of that enclosed region.

Fix a named, positively oriented SI laboratory chart with coordinates

coordinate units of the laboratory convention: $c>0$ is in m s$^{-1}$,
$k_0:=\omega/c$ is in m$^{-1}$, and electric-field components are in V
m$^{-1}$. Let
$\Pi=\{(x,y,z_0):(x,y)\in D\}$ be a specified reference plane, where
$z_0\in\mathbb R$ and $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a specified nonempty region.
Its oriented orthonormal transverse basis is $(e_x,e_y)$ and its normal is
$e_z$.

For the paraxial context, adopt $c>0$, $k_0=\omega/c$, and
$0<\delta<1$. The angular-spectrum variable $\xi\in\mathbb R^2$ is measured
in cycles per metre, $q=2\pi\xi$ is in m$^{-1}$, and the forward propagating
cone is $D_\delta=\{\xi:|q|\le\delta k_0\}$ with
$k_z(\xi)=\sqrt{k_0^2-|q|^2}>0$. The matrix below is defined pointwise for the
two-component projection; it does not assert that an arbitrary random
superposition is an exact Maxwell field or that the individual-mode
longitudinal bound extends to an ensemble without additional hypotheses.

Let $(\Xi,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ be a specified probability space. At each
fixed $\rho\in D$, let $Z_\rho:\Xi\to\mathbb C^2$ be measurable, with four real
coordinates
$X_\rho=(\operatorname{Re}Z_x,\operatorname{Im}Z_x,
\operatorname{Re}Z_y,\operatorname{Im}Z_y)$ forming a square-integrable
$\mathbb R^4$ random vector and
$\mathbb E[|Z_x(\rho)|^2+|Z_y(\rho)|^2]<\infty$. For $\sigma\in\Xi$, the
associated transverse real-field model is
$E_\perp(\rho,\sigma,t)=\operatorname{Re}(Z_\rho(\sigma)e^{-i\omega t})$.
Expectation is taken over this declared classical ensemble and is applied
componentwise to complex integrable variables. Define
$$\Gamma(\rho):=\mathbb E[Z_\rho Z_\rho^\dagger],\qquad \Gamma_{ij}(\rho):=\mathbb E[Z_i(\rho)\overline{Z_j(\rho)}]\quad(i,j\in\{1,2\}).$$
Thus $\Gamma$ is the uncentered second-moment matrix of the two selected
components; no zero-mean assumption is made. The degree of polarization is
defined only when $S_0>0$ by
$$S_0:=\Gamma_{11}+\Gamma_{22},\quad S_1:=\Gamma_{11}-\Gamma_{22},\quad S_2:=2\operatorname{Re}\Gamma_{12},\quad S_3:=-2\operatorname{Im}\Gamma_{12},\qquad \mathcal P:=\frac{\sqrt{S_1^2+S_2^2+S_3^2}}{S_0}.$$
The minus sign in $S_3$ is fixed by the stated phasor convention and the
ordered basis $(e_x,e_y)$. In this two-component model, a positive-intensity
state is called unpolarized when $\Gamma=(S_0/2)I_2$; this label concerns
second moments and does not say that any realization is a quantum state.
The $S_j$ have units (V m$^{-1}$)$^2$; $S_0$ is a mean-square field coordinate,
not an absolutely calibrated irradiance.

The construction applies to any ordered pair of square-integrable classical
complex amplitudes. When the pair labels transverse electric components,
$S_j$ have the polarization interpretation just defined. When it labels two
beam channels, the same matrix entries are channel correlations; they are not
polarization components.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

For $v=(v_1,v_2)^{\mathsf T}$, the finite sum
$\overline{v_1}Z_1+\overline{v_2}Z_2$ has an integrable squared modulus,
because it is bounded by
$2(|v_1|^2|Z_1|^2+|v_2|^2|Z_2|^2)$. Expanding the finite matrix product
therefore gives $v^\dagger\Gamma v
=\mathbb E[|v^\dagger Z|^2]\ge0$. Hence $\Gamma$ is positive semidefinite.

Write $\Gamma=\begin{pmatrix}a&c\\\overline c&b\end{pmatrix}$, where
$a,b\ge0$. If $a>0$, positivity applied to $v=(-c/a,1)^{\mathsf T}$ gives
$b-|c|^2/a\ge0$, hence $ab\ge|c|^2$. If $a=0$ and $c\ne0$, positivity at
$v=(-tc,1)^{\mathsf T}$ gives $b-2t|c|^2\ge0$ for every $t>0$, which fails
for sufficiently large $t$; thus $c=0$ and again $ab\ge|c|^2$.

The definitions give
$S_0^2-S_1^2=4ab$ and $S_2^2+S_3^2=4|c|^2$. Step 2.1 therefore proves
$S_0^2\ge S_1^2+S_2^2+S_3^2$. Equality is equivalent to
$\det\Gamma=ab-|c|^2=0$, which for a positive-semidefinite $2\times2$ matrix
means rank below two; it is rank zero exactly when $\Gamma=0$, and otherwise
rank one. When $S_0>0$, taking nonnegative square roots gives
$0\le\mathcal P\le1$; when $S_0=0$ the quotient is undefined by its
Definition.

Since $M$ is fixed, $(MZ)(MZ)^\dagger=MZZ^\dagger M^\dagger$ for every
realization. Taking the componentwise expectation and using [F2]'s linearity
gives $\Gamma'=\mathbb E[(MZ)(MZ)^\dagger]=M\Gamma M^\dagger$.

Expectation is taken over this declared classical ensemble and is applied
componentwise to complex integrable variables. Define
$$\Gamma(\rho):=\mathbb E[Z_\rho Z_\rho^\dagger],\qquad \Gamma_{ij}(\rho):=\mathbb E[Z_i(\rho)\overline{Z_j(\rho)}]\quad(i,j\in\{1,2\}).$$
Thus $\Gamma$ is the uncentered second-moment matrix of the two selected
components; no zero-mean assumption is made. The degree of polarization is
defined only when $S_0>0$ by
$$S_0:=\Gamma_{11}+\Gamma_{22},\quad S_1:=\Gamma_{11}-\Gamma_{22},\quad S_2:=2\operatorname{Re}\Gamma_{12},\quad S_3:=-2\operatorname{Im}\Gamma_{12},\qquad \mathcal P:=\frac{\sqrt{S_1^2+S_2^2+S_3^2}}{S_0}.$$
The minus sign in $S_3$ is fixed by the stated phasor convention and the
ordered basis $(e_x,e_y)$. In this two-component model, a positive-intensity
state is called unpolarized when $\Gamma=(S_0/2)I_2$; this label concerns
second moments and does not say that any realization is a quantum state.
The $S_j$ have units (V m$^{-1}$)$^2$; $S_0$ is a mean-square field coordinate,
not an absolutely calibrated irradiance.

The construction applies to any ordered pair of square-integrable classical
complex amplitudes. When the pair labels transverse electric components,
$S_j$ have the polarization interpretation just defined. When it labels two
beam channels, the same matrix entries are channel correlations; they are not
polarization components.
